docs.title: The Ember Age
docs.text:
A homebrew Star Wars campaign for FFG (Edge of the Empire / Age of Rebellion / Force and Destiny)

Hope with rust on it.

When ~910 BBY. In-world, the year 90 AR — After Ruusan. What Ninety years after the Jedi and Sith annihilated each other at Ruusan, the galaxy has withered into ten thousand islands — and the war is passing out of human living memory. Now the Force is returning, the beacons are relighting, and what comes next has not been decided. Who The player characters are wayfinders — a crew of seekers, traders, diplomats, and perhaps one of the newly Force-sensitive — reopening the galaxy one lane at a time. Tone Hope with rust on it. Rebuilding and discovery. Light and dark finding a way forward together — or the old dogmas returning wearing new faces.

The thesis of the era, and the line to say aloud at session zero:

Nobody broke the galaxy — everyone just stopped holding it up.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
• The Withering — the ninety-year timeline from Ruusan to the relighting of Vesta-9.
  • The Galaxy at 90 AR — travel, memory, salvage, and the two networks that never stopped running.
  • Factions — six answers to "what comes next," and two standing powers.
  • The Awakening — the Force is coming back, and nobody knows why.
  • Campaign Structure — three acts: Reconnection, Convergence, the Founding.
  • Session One: "The Light on Vesta-9" — the cold open.
  • Mechanics — character creation, Obligation, Lore Fragments, beacon relighting, and the Force in the Ember Age.
  • Terms of the Era — the appendix glossary.

Players: mind the seals

Everything in this wiki's player edition can be shared as it is discovered in play. The GM section exists only in the GM build of this site — if you can see a "GM" tab in the navigation, you are reading the GM edition. Players never see that page.

docs.title: About this campaign and canon
docs.text:
This campaign diverges from Legends canon nowhere at all. The record says the Republic and the Jedi Order endured from Ruusan to the prequel era — but records are written by recoveries, and institutions that outlive their crises remember themselves as unbroken. The thought bomb beheaded two institutions in an afternoon; that both were eventually refounded does not mean either was alive in between. The thousand years of peace the prequels remember includes these decades. The Bane novels remain true, and so does everything published after — this era is simply the chapter nobody wrote down.

Your table writes it.

docs.title: Campaign Structure
docs.text:
Three acts. Three mechanics. Three questions.

Act Sessions Shape Core mechanic The question Act 1 — Reconnection ~1–8 Episodic Obligation (survival) What did the galaxy become while nobody was looking? Act 2 — Convergence ~9–16 Hinge events, any order Morality (conscience) Every government has a policy now — what's yours? Act 3 — The Founding ~17–20+ Two summits and one canyon Duty (cause) What comes next — and who decides?

Players discover this as they play

The act summaries below are shareable as the table reaches them. The GM's private notes live elsewhere.

Start here: Session One — "The Light on Vesta-9". Track play in the Session Log.

docs.title: Act 1 — Reconnection
docs.text:
Sessions ~1–8. Episodic. Each relit beacon opens a corridor, and each corridor holds a world that spent ninety years becoming something strange.

Act goals: meet all five factions on the ground, gather lore fragments, and let the crew's reputation outrun them.

docs.title: Episode seeds beyond Vesta-9
docs.text:
1. The Sealed Enclave. A Vigil-sealed temple whose caretaker droid still runs lessons for empty rooms — and something answered this year's roll call.
  2. The Ration Engine. A world administered for ninety years by a droid bureaucracy that refuses to believe the galaxy is back; the crew must out-argue a spreadsheet that genuinely loves its people.
  3. The Mausoleum Yards. A mothballed Republic fleet, now a hull-city of squatters, with an Admiralty prize crew inbound carrying eviction orders.
  4. The Memory Market. A world where provenance is currency, and a forgery ring is quietly poisoning the galaxy's lore-fragment economy — including, perhaps, something the party already trusts.
  5. The Oracle of Brel. A settlement worships a Force-sensitive child whose true dreams are eating her sleep; three factions arrive the same week the PCs do.
  6. The Scar. A New Sith Wars battlefield where the dark side pooled. An Inheritor dig site offers the crew coin, answers, and the campaign's first real temptation.
  7. The Five Systems. A small confederation that is, embarrassingly, thriving in isolation. Plugging them into the galaxy may ruin them — and they know it. Discovery is not neutral.
  8. The Toll. A Hutt successor cartel holds the only living chokepoint lane and sells passage; the diplomats and traders get their spotlight episode.
  9. The Dead Letter. An assassin droid is still working a ninety-year-old contract list. The government that posted it is dust, the Guild's purists insist a posting is a posting, and the next name on the list is somebody the crew needs alive.
  10. The Handoff. A Kajidic middleman's "cargo" turns out to be a Force-sensitive child, sold up the chain toward buyers nobody names aloud. Intercepting the shipment is the easy part; deciding what to do about the market it revealed is the episode.

docs.title: Act 2 — Convergence
docs.text:
Sessions ~9–16. The quiet ends.

Hinge events, playable in any order:

docs.title: The Awakening goes public
docs.text: A display of the Force too public to hush — now every government has a policy, and every policy has victims.

docs.title: The Conclave of Charts
docs.text: The Lamplighters auction the relighting order. Every faction bids; the party holds swing data from Act 1.

docs.title: The Unveiling
docs.text: The Inheritors present a trained cadre — the first "Sith" seen since Ruusan. They are costume: real techniques, counterfeit lineage. Almost nobody alive can tell the difference, and the two beings who can have just been handed an address.

docs.title: The Vigil breaks
docs.text: The argument over custody of the Force-sensitive goes from doctrinal to armed, and both halves of the Vigil come to the party for help.

docs.title: The Annexation
docs.text: The Admiralty "secures" a relit corridor for everyone's safety, and does not leave.

docs.title: Act 3 — The Founding
docs.text: Sessions ~17–20+. Two summits and one canyon.

docs.title: The Founding Conclave
docs.text:
Crisis forces the constitutional moment: Republic restored, Admiralty empire, a concord of independent leagues — or the players' own third way. Their accumulated fragments, favors, and Force-sensitive allies are the votes.

And hanging over the whole chamber is a legal fact almost nobody remembers: three Masters, met in a temple, can reconvene the Jedi Council — and who counts as a Master, ninety years out of session, is a question worth a war.

docs.title: The Valley of the Jedi
docs.text:
Whoever brings the new Force-sensitives here defines what the Force's return means. On the table:

  • Release the thousand bound souls.
  • Draw on them.
  • Seal the Valley for another age.
  • Or ask the souls what they want.

docs.title: The true ending
docs.text: The campaign's true ending is the pairing of a political outcome with a Valley choice. An empire that frees the dead and a republic that feeds on them are both possible, and both worth playing to find out.

docs.title: Session Log
docs.text: One entry per session. Copy the template; the ledger below it is the campaign's memory.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
## Session N — TITLE (date)

**Where:** system / world / beacon
**Obligation triggered:** whose, and how it bit
**Beacons:** relit / attempted / learned of
**Fragments gained:** name — tag (Jedi/Sith/Civic) — bears on Question…
**Factions moved:** who noticed the crew, and what they now want
**Debts & favors:** who owes whom
**XP awarded:**
**The line of the night:**

docs.title: Ledger
docs.text:
# Title Beacons Fragments Faction heat 1 The Light on Vesta-9 Vesta-9 relit (witnessed) — Vigil, Admiralty, Lamplighters — three factions know the crew's name

(Add a row per session; write the full entry above it.)

docs.title: Cold open
docs.text: The crew is grounded at Okrent's Drift, a fuel-depot port at the frayed end of a living lane — cargo impounded, Obligations circling — when the sky changes. Vesta-9, dark for sixty years, is broadcasting. Every ship that can lift is lifting.

docs.title: Scene 1 — The Scramble
docs.text: Get off-world first: the impound, the fuel, and a likable rival crew worth keeping as recurring foils.

docs.title: Scene 2 — The Race
docs.text: Astrogation on a decayed route. Introduce fragments here, when one page of somebody's grandmother's rutter is the difference between arrival and drift.

docs.title: Scene 3 — The Beacon
docs.text:
Vesta-9 station, lit and humming — and occupied.

  • Keeper Adressa Vhail of the Vigil is praying at the beacon core and will not say how she got there.
  • The Admiralty sloop Steadfast (Cmdr. Joss Reike) drops in demanding all vessels stand to for inspection.
  • Chartmistress Bel Nerra of the Lamplighters arrives to certify the relight — and to hire witnesses.

docs.title: Scene 4 — The Stowaway
docs.text:
Mid-standoff, the crew finds Immi Ozha, twelve, asleep in their hold, dreaming loudly of a canyon full of light. The beacon flickers in rhythm with her breathing.

  • Reike wants her manifested and registered.
  • Vhail goes very quiet.
  • Nerra offers papers on the spot.

docs.title: Out
docs.text: The corridor to the Q'ell Reach stands open — Act 1's episode worlds lie beyond — three factions know the crew's name, and someone knows exactly what just happened.

docs.title: Factions
docs.text: Six answers to the question "what comes next," then two standing powers not in the race but impossible to ignore. Each entry: who they are, what they want, what they offer a wayfinder crew, and the crack running through them.

docs.title: The six answers
docs.text: Faction What comes next Offers the crew The crack The Provisional Republic Continuity — the old flag restored Accreditation, archive access, moral cover Custodians of the idea, terrified of being tested The Admiralty Naval protection — which is to say control Escort, fuel, repair, genuine safety Their founding story requires an enemy The Vigil Veneration without practice, forever Sanctuary, authentication, sealed places The newly Force-sensitive split them in half The Inheritors A monopoly on the returning Force Real training, when no one else can teach They don't know whose hand is at the top The Lamplighters The network relit — in the order they choose Charters, salvage rights, first-lighting fees Whoever sets the order decides the century The Kajidics Nothing, thank you — scarcity is margin Fuel, parts, black-lane rutters, no questions The young Hutts have run the numbers

docs.title: The two standing powers
docs.text: Power Position To the crew The Bounty Hunters' Guild The posting is the one writ that still travels Employer, threat, and the only enforcement a promise has The Mandalorian Clans War is work; foundlings are foundlings The finest soldiers alive, and everyone's contingency plan

docs.title: The Admiralty
docs.text: The government of the Bastion Worlds — the last power with working capital ships.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text:
The shipyard cluster where the fleet that refused the demobilization order dropped anchor and never left. A stratocracy built by that squadron — its current Lady Admiral is the granddaughter of the woman who said no — grown into the last power with working capital ships.

The distinction matters on the ground: Bastioners are fiercely proud of their worlds and considerably less fond of the uniforms that run them, and the Admiralty works hard to keep outsiders from seeing the difference.

docs.title: What they want
docs.text: The relit lanes placed under naval protection — which is to say under naval control. And they conscript.

docs.title: What they offer a wayfinder crew
docs.text: What no one else can: escort, fuel, repair, genuine safety. Their pitch lands because it is half true: the Republic's weakness invited the wars.

docs.title: The crack
docs.text: Their founding story requires an enemy, and if the Sith do not return, some of their officers will need them to.

docs.title: The Bounty Hunters' Guild
docs.text: A standing power — the closest thing the galaxy has to interstellar law.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text:
When the courts stopped reaching across systems, one writ kept traveling: the posting. The Guild honors any bounty whose bond clears — governments, Kajidics, grieving families, it does not care — and its code (deliver as posted, no poaching, the posting is sacred) has made it, absurdly, the closest thing the galaxy has to interstellar law.

Worlds too small for judges hire hunters as circuit arbiters.

docs.title: The dark side of the code
docs.text: Postings outlive their posters, and Guild purists still honor bounties filed by governments that no longer exist.

docs.title: To a wayfinder crew
docs.text: The Guild is employer, threat, and occasionally the only enforcement a promise has.

docs.title: The Inheritors
docs.text: A patient whisper-network selling the era's most dangerous currency: answers.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text: Founded by the Brotherhood's surviving quartermasters, collaborators, and camp-followers — some of them still alive — the network has spent three generations quietly hoarding Sith lore, and, lately, arriving first on the doorsteps of frightened Force-sensitive families with answers, flattery, and coin.

docs.title: What they want
docs.text: A monopoly on the returning Force.

docs.title: What they offer a wayfinder crew
docs.text: The era's most dangerous currency: real training, when no one else alive can teach.

docs.title: The crack
docs.text:
Even senior Inheritors are not sure whose hand is at the top of their own organization — whether they serve a living tradition or are merely wearing its costume.

(The GM knows the answer.)

docs.title: The Kajidics
docs.text: The Hutt clan-corporations — the one interstellar institution the Withering made stronger.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text: They never needed the Republic; scarcity is margin. They run the black lanes (the unregistered routes that never went dark), the fuel and scrap monopolies, and the protection rackets that pass for civic order on a hundred worlds.

docs.title: What they want
docs.text: Their answer to "what comes next" is nothing, thank you — they will be paid to keep it that way, because every relit beacon on a route they do not control is competition.

docs.title: What they offer a wayfinder crew
docs.text:
What no charter can:

  • Fuel and parts.
  • Black-lane rutters.
  • Cash work with no questions attached.

docs.title: The crack
docs.text: Generational: the young Hutts have run the numbers and think a rebuilt galaxy pays better than scarcity rents ever will, and a clan war over that spreadsheet is one bad season away.

docs.title: The Lamplighters
docs.text: The beacon-tenders' guild — nominally neutral, universally necessary.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text: Chartkeepers, rutter-brokers, and lane-runners who never stopped maintaining what could be maintained. The natural patron for a wayfinder crew.

docs.title: What they want
docs.text: The network relit — in the order they choose.

docs.title: What they offer a wayfinder crew
docs.text:
• Charters.
  • Salvage rights.
  • First-lighting fees for every beacon reopened (see Relighting a Beacon).

docs.title: The crack
docs.text: Whoever sets the relighting order decides which worlds matter for the next century. The Grandmaster of Charts knows this, every faction knows she knows, and her neutrality is not unpurchasable — the price is merely very high.

docs.title: The Mandalorian Clans
docs.text: A standing power — the one people who never demobilized.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text: Rebuilt under a Mandalore into clan companies that hire out to anyone whose bond clears — which, in a disarmed galaxy, makes them the finest soldiers alive and everyone's contingency plan. They remember the wars differently than everyone else: as work.

docs.title: On the Awakening
docs.text:
They hold the era's strangest position, which is no position at all — the clans take foundlings from every ruin they are paid to make or guard, and a foundling who bends luck is simply a promising warrior.

Nobody is watching the one culture that neither fears the gifted nor wants to own them.

docs.title: The Provisional Republic
docs.text: The rump Senate and its Archive bureaus, ninety years into an interregnum they still call temporary.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text: They hold unmatched legitimacy, unmatched documentation, a handful of long-lived senators who personally remember the Republic whole — and a writ that ends at the atmosphere.

docs.title: What they want
docs.text: Every relit beacon registered under Republic charter, restoring the galaxy as a matter of continuity rather than conquest.

docs.title: What they offer a wayfinder crew
docs.text:
• Letters of accreditation.
  • Archive access — the richest source of Civic lore fragments.
  • The moral cover of the old flag.

docs.title: The crack
docs.text: Ninety years of "provisional" has bred leaders who prefer custodianship of the idea to the risk of actually governing — the institution has learned to survive by never being tested.

docs.title: The Vigil
docs.text: Keepers of everything the old orders left behind — and the standing peace terms with the bereaved.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text:
Founded by Ruusan's grave-tenders and the Jedi Order's lay custodians, deeded the sealed temples and relics by the Council's last act — custody of property, though nothing in the minutes grants them custody of the calling. An angry galaxy tolerates them precisely because they keep it all locked away; their doctrine is not only theology, it is the standing peace terms with the bereaved.

Their founding generation — the last people who actually knew Jedi — is dying, and doctrine is hardening exactly as fast as memory fails.

docs.title: What they want
docs.text: They gather relics, authenticate artifacts, tend the Valley of the Jedi — and forbid, absolutely, the use of any of it. Veneration without practice, so that the fire can never spread again.

docs.title: What they offer a wayfinder crew
docs.text:
• Sanctuary.
  • Authentication of artifacts and lore fragments.
  • Access to sealed places no one else may enter.

docs.title: The crack
docs.text:
The newly Force-sensitive: half the order sees sacrilege walking around in children's bodies, and half sees the Order reborn and weeps. That argument will not stay doctrinal forever.

And beneath it sits the deed itself: their authority covers stone and relic, not flesh — a distinction somebody is eventually going to read aloud.

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text:
FFG Star Wars (Edge of the Empire / Age of Rebellion / Force and Destiny), with the Ember Age's own subsystems on top.

The three core mechanics mirror the three acts — survival, then conscience, then cause:

Mechanic When Why Obligation From session zero It is a broke, indebted galaxy Morality Force-sensitive PCs, from session zero See The Force in the Ember Age Duty Held in reserve until Act 3 When the party formally aligns with a founding vision

docs.title: The Ember Age subsystems
docs.text:
• Lore Fragments — the core subsystem: assemble the true history yourselves.
  • Relighting a Beacon — the set-piece skill challenge.
  • The Force in the Ember Age — Wellsprings, witnesses, and Morality without a Council.
  • Ships of the Ember Age — the heirloom lane-runner and the hulls of 90 AR.

Start with Character Creation.

docs.title: Relighting a Beacon
docs.text: The set-piece skill challenge. Three stages in any order, built so different PCs shine.

docs.title: 1. Wake it
docs.text: Mechanics or Computers against sixty years of dead-man failsafes.

docs.title: 2. Chart it
docs.text: Hard Astrogation, with fragments and rutters as boost dice.

docs.title: 3. Speak to it
docs.text: A Knowledge or social check to satisfy old Republic handshake protocols — or to convince a guild observer to certify the lighting.

docs.title: What a relit beacon does
docs.text:
Each relit beacon:

  • Opens a region — a corridor of worlds ninety years strange.
  • Shifts the faction map.
  • Pays a first-lighting fee (see the Lamplighters).
  • Raises the same question: who follows you through?

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
• Standard starting XP. Any career from any of the three core books (Edge of the Empire, Age of Rebellion, Force and Destiny).
  • The crew shares one heirloom ship — a Wayfarer-class, or any YT or Ghtroc hull reflavored as a pre-Ruusan lane-runner, a century old and held together by devotion. See Ships of the Ember Age.
  • Everyone takes Obligation — it is a broke, indebted galaxy.
  • Force-sensitive PCs also track Morality.
  • Duty waits until Act 3, when the party formally aligns with a founding vision. The three mechanics mirror the three acts: survival, then conscience, then cause.

docs.title: Playing one of the Awakened
docs.text:
A Force-sensitive PC enters via the Force-Sensitive Exile or Force-Sensitive Emergent universal specializations, or any Force and Destiny career, at Force Rating 1 — with no living teacher.

Their growth runs through discovery, not tuition: see The Force in the Ember Age. Knowledge is treasure.

docs.title: Wayfinder crew concepts
docs.text: The party are wayfinders — scout-envoy-archaeologists reopening the galaxy one lane at a time. Any concept that answers "why does this person reopen dead lanes?" works: seekers, traders, diplomats, chartkeepers, salvage crews, interpreters (splintered Basic makes them load-bearing), couriers off the swoop circuit, and perhaps one of the newly Force-sensitive.

docs.title: The Force in the Ember Age
docs.text: In this era the Force is not a skill; it is an event.

docs.title: Almost no teachers — Wellsprings
docs.text:
Increasing Force Rating or opening a new power tree requires a Wellspring found in play — a functional holocron, a vergence, or, rarest of all, a living mentor from one of the hidden lineages — in addition to the usual XP.

Knowledge is treasure.

docs.title: Witnesses
docs.text:
Open Force use in front of ordinary people:

  • Shifts their disposition one step — awe or fear, GM's call.
  • Adds a setback die to social checks with that community until the party addresses what they saw.

docs.title: Morality
docs.text: Run it as written, but land the aftermath of Conflict harder: there are no counselors, no Council, no one to tell a Force-sensitive what the nightmares mean — except whoever reached them first.

docs.title: Lore Fragments
docs.text: The core subsystem. The players assemble the true history themselves.

docs.title: What a fragment is
docs.text:
A fragment is a tangible source: a holocron shard, a rutter, a sealed archive cell, an unwiped pre-war droid memory core — or a living witness. The last human eyewitnesses of Ruusan are dying this decade, and longer-lived species still carry the war as personal memory; testimony is a fragment you can argue with, and it contradicts the documents exactly as often as they contradict each other.

Every fragment carries a tag — Jedi, Sith, or Civic — and fragments about the same event from different tags always disagree on one load-bearing fact.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: • Holding a relevant fragment adds a boost die to related Knowledge checks.

docs.title: Reconstruction
docs.text:
With three or more fragments bearing on one named Question ("What ended the Order?" "What is the Valley?"), the party may attempt a Hard Knowledge (Lore) check as a group scene.

  • If all three tags are represented: upgrade an ability die once.
  • If only one tag is represented: upgrade the difficulty once — bias is real.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Result Effect Success The GM reveals a Truth, and the party gains an Insight — permanently remove a setback die from one defined category of checks, or unlock an out-of-career talent purchase the Truth justifies Triumph A secret beyond the Question Despair A corrupted conclusion enters play — and the party believes it

docs.title: Named Questions
docs.text:
Keep a public list of the Questions the party is working, e.g.:

  • What ended the Order?
  • What is the Valley?
  • Who lit Vesta-9?
  • What did the Adjournment actually adjourn?

(GM: track issued fragments and their tags in the GM tools section of this wiki.)

docs.title: Obligation, Reflavored
docs.text:
Roll or choose. Everyone takes one — it is a broke, indebted galaxy.

d10 Obligation The Ember Age version 1 Debt Sector scrip or a Kajidic marker, ruinous interest 2 Family You are an isolated homeworld's only link 3 Oath To a dying archivist 4 Notice An Admiralty conscription writ with your name on it 5 Secret Someone knows you are Force-sensitive — or love someone who is 6 Obsession One fragment you cannot let go 7 Responsibility Refugees from a lane that died 8 Contract The Lamplighters hold your ship's papers 9 Posted A Guild bounty, still live, with your name on it 10 Choose or invent Keep it era-true: debts, memory, and the people a dead lane stranded

Run Obligation as written in the core rules (starting totals, triggers, strain effects at threshold). The reflavoring changes who comes knocking, not the math.

docs.title: Ships of the Ember Age
docs.text:
Ninety years after Ruusan, nothing flies new. Every hull in this file is an inheritance — a pre-Withering pattern kept alive by devotion, cannibalized cousins, and a family's whole savings — and the handful of yards that could lay a fresh keel are strategic prizes worth wars. Book prices are quoted in old Republic credits as printed; in 90 AR a working ship is beyond price and a dead one becomes a neighborhood. Every stat block below is an official FFG vehicle block reproduced as printed; only the names and the rust are ours.

This file is player-safe: no campaign secrets appear anywhere in it.

docs.title: The Heirloom Lane-Runners
docs.text: Campaign convention. The three hulls below are the campaign's "lane-runner patterns" — freighter designs that were already old when the beacons went dark, reflavored as pre-Ruusan keels a century deep in one family's service. A player crew's shared ship uses one of these blocks exactly as printed: age lives in the paint, the smell, and the Obligation, never in the numbers. If a GM wants the rust mechanically visible for a session, RAW offers the Inferior quality (on a weapon: −1 damage and automatic threat on checks using it; on another system, apply the automatic threat) as a temporary, story-driven condition — apply it as a scene complication and take it off when the crew earns the repair montage. The blocks themselves stay stock.

docs.title: Wayfarer-class Medium Transport
docs.text:
Vehicle — heirloom lane-runner — the deep-hold pattern

A hammer-headed hauler with a detachable cargo section big enough to carry a village's whole harvest — which, most years, is exactly what it carries.

Silhouette Speed Handling 5 3 −2

Defense Fore/Port/Starboard/Aft 1/1/1/2 · Armor 4 · Hull Trauma Threshold 32 · System Strain Threshold 20

  • Hyperdrive: Primary: Class 2, Backup: Class 14
  • Navicomputer: Yes
  • Sensor Range: Short
  • Crew: One pilot, one co-pilot, one engineer, one cargo master, six crew
  • Encumbrance Capacity: 850 · Passenger Capacity: 6
  • Consumables: Three months · Price/Rarity: 120,000 credits/5 · Customization Hard Points: 5
  • Weapons: Dorsal turret-mounted quad laser cannon "the Lodge Gun" (Fire Arc Forward; Damage 5; Critical 3; Range [Close]; Accurate 1, Linked 3)

Chassis: Wayfarer-class Medium Transport, Edge of the Empire Core Rulebook (adjustments: none). (one oddity to verify against print: a turret mount with Fire Arc Forward is as transcribed — if your copy prints a wider arc, the book wins) Era notes: A century old, held together by devotion — the detachable hold has outlived three drive sections, and the current one is the "new part" (it is forty). Scarcity flavor only; the block is stock. Using it: The Wayfarer is the crew-as-community ship: ten berths, a hold worth robbing, and handling that makes every pirate encounter a negotiation first. Its aft shields are its best — this pattern was built to run, not fight — so chases end scenes better than broadsides do.

docs.title: Ghtroc 720 Freighter
docs.text:
Vehicle — heirloom lane-runner — the shell-back pattern

Rim spacers call the pattern "the turtle": ugly, patient, and famously hard to kill, which is why so many of them are still flying and so many prettier ships are reefs.

Silhouette Speed Handling 4 3 −1

Defense Fore/Aft 1/1 · Armor 5 · Hull Trauma Threshold 28 · System Strain Threshold 15

  • Hyperdrive: Primary: Class 2, Backup: Class 15
  • Navicomputer: Yes
  • Sensor Range: Medium
  • Crew: One pilot, one co-pilot
  • Encumbrance Capacity: 200 · Passenger Capacity: 10
  • Consumables: Two months · Price/Rarity: 112,000 credits/8 · Customization Hard Points: 4
  • Weapons: Dorsal turret-mounted twin light laser cannon "Grandmother's Argument" (Fire Arc All; Damage 5; Critical 3; Range [Close]; Linked 1)

Chassis: Ghtroc 720 Light Freighter, Edge of the Empire Core Rulebook (adjustments: none). Era notes: Ghtroc Industries died before the Withering did; every 720 alive is a hand-me-down, and its printed rarity is the era in one number. Flavor only; the block is stock. Using it: The 720 is the ship for crews who expect to be shot at and plan to be boring about it: armor 5 and twenty-eight hull make it the closest thing a wayfinder can own to a bunker. Ten passenger berths make it the natural refugee boat, pilgrim carrier, or mobile village — which is its own kind of plot hook.

docs.title: YT-1300 Light Freighter
docs.text:
Vehicle — heirloom lane-runner — the everywhere pattern

Corellia built so many of these before the lights went out that the design has become a kind of shared memory: every port has one, and every one is somebody's whole inheritance.

Silhouette Speed Handling 4 3 −1

Defense Fore/Aft 1/1 · Armor 3 · Hull Trauma Threshold 22 · System Strain Threshold 15

  • Hyperdrive: Primary: Class 2, Backup: Class 12
  • Navicomputer: Yes
  • Sensor Range: Short
  • Crew: One pilot, one co-pilot/engineer
  • Encumbrance Capacity: 165 · Passenger Capacity: 6
  • Consumables: Two months · Price/Rarity: 100,000 credits/4 · Customization Hard Points: 6
  • Weapons: One dorsal and one ventral turret-mounted medium laser cannon (Fire Arc All; Damage 6; Critical 3; Range [Close])

Chassis: YT-1300 Light Freighter, Edge of the Empire Core Rulebook (adjustments: none). Era notes: The six hard points are the point: ninety years of owners have each left one modification and one regret in the crawlspaces. Any "custom gear" a family installed is bought with the printed hard points at RAW cost — never free. Using it: The YT-1300 rewards a two-hander crew — pilot flying, partner bouncing between turret and engine room. It is the fastest of the three patterns to turn around in port, which makes it the smuggler's and courier's pick; its thin armor means the pilot's talents are the real defensive stat.

docs.title: BNS Steadfast, Bastion-pattern Patrol Sloop
docs.text:
Vehicle — the Admiralty — Commander Joss Reike's inspection sloop

The Steadfast does not hail you so much as inform you: a wall of pre-Ruusan naval steel that was keeping this watch before your grandmother was born, crewed by people who never stopped believing in uniforms.

Silhouette Speed Handling 5 3 −1

Defense Fore/Port/Starboard/Aft 2/2/2/1 · Armor 6 · Hull Trauma Threshold 45 · System Strain Threshold 20

  • Hyperdrive: None
  • Navicomputer: None
  • Sensor Range: Long
  • Crew: Twelve
  • Encumbrance Capacity: not listed in the printed block · Passenger Capacity: 10 (troopers or prisoners)
  • Consumables: One month · Price/Rarity: 4,000,000 credits/5 · Customization Hard Points: 2
  • Weapons:
  • Dorsal, ventral, port, and starboard turret-mounted point-defense turbolaser batteries (Fire Arc All; Damage 11; Critical 3; Range [Long]; Breach 3, Linked 1, Slow-Firing 1)
  • Forward-mounted concussion missile launcher (Fire Arc Forward; Damage 7; Critical 3; Range [Short]; Blast 4, Breach 4, Guided 3, Slow-Firing 1)

Chassis: Imperial System Patrol Craft (IPV-1), Beyond the Rim (adjustments: none — the printed block lists no encumbrance capacity; the line above reports that fact rather than inventing a number). (stats unverified against print — scope: every other line of this block verified against the printed IPV-1; the one unverified field is Price/Rarity — check the printed block for the figure and restore the "(R)" restricted marker if the print carries one, as a military hull likely does) Era notes: Bastion-pattern sloops carry no hyperdrive as printed — the Admiralty ferries them between systems clamped to fleet tenders, which is why one can "drop in" on a beacon relight and why, once on station, it is never leaving until the tender comes back. Maintenance is the one thing the Bastion yards still do perfectly; this is the rare hull in the era with nothing patched. Using it: The Steadfast is a wall, not a duel — its turbolasers outrange and outhit anything a wayfinder crew owns, so the scene it creates is procedural: stand to, present manifests, submit to boarding (those ten passenger berths are Reike's inspection party, or your cell). Let the players win against the paperwork, the commander's rigidity, or the tender schedule, never the guns. If they run, Speed 3 and Handling −1 give a bold pilot honest odds; being remembered by the Admiralty is the real cost.

docs.title: Swoop Bike
docs.text:
Vehicle — the swoop circuit — mail, gossip, and glory at 600 kph

The circuit is the closest thing the galaxy has to a broadcast, and this is its transmitter: one screaming engine, one rider, and a courier satchel bolted where the sense should be.

Silhouette Speed Handling 2 3 +2

Defense Fore/Aft 0/0 · Armor 0 · Hull Trauma Threshold 2 · System Strain Threshold 3

  • Hyperdrive: None
  • Navicomputer: None
  • Sensor Range: None
  • Crew: One pilot
  • Encumbrance Capacity: 4 · Passenger Capacity: 1
  • Consumables: None · Price/Rarity: 6,000 credits/3 · Customization Hard Points: 2 · Maximum Altitude: 350 meters
  • Weapons: None

Chassis: Flare-S Swoop, Edge of the Empire Core Rulebook (adjustments: none). (stats unverified against print — scope: Speed/Handling and Hull Trauma/System Strain Thresholds could not be independently corroborated — verify them against the Flare-S Swoop entry in the Edge of the Empire Core Rulebook vehicles chapter before table use; the remaining fields are corroborated as printed) Era notes: Circuit machines are shrines of mismatched relic parts, each with a dead racer's name painted somewhere honest. Sponsorship livery (Kajidic, Lamplighter, hometown collective) is worth a boost die on the social checks it impresses — never on the flying. Using it: Hull trauma 2 means any solid hit ends a swoop, so run races and chases as pure Piloting (Planetary) drama — opposed checks, terrain, nerve — where crashing out is the stake rather than damage math. A circuit rider is also the era's newsfeed: whoever wins the season carries the rumors, the mail, and quietly the contraband, which makes befriending one worth more than beating one.

docs.title: Kajidic Fuel Barge
docs.text:
Vehicle — the Kajidics — a rolling monopoly with a Hutt's name on the manifest

A hundred meters of tank and rivet moving at the speed of contract law. It is slow, unarmed, and utterly safe, because everyone for ten systems needs what is inside it to arrive.

Silhouette Speed Handling 5 2 −3

Defense Fore/Port/Starboard/Aft 2/1/1/1 · Armor 2 · Hull Trauma Threshold 40 · System Strain Threshold 20

  • Hyperdrive: Primary: Class 3, Backup: Class 20
  • Navicomputer: Yes
  • Sensor Range: Medium
  • Crew: 20
  • Encumbrance Capacity: 10,000 · Passenger Capacity: 5
  • Consumables: Three months · Price/Rarity: 200,000 credits/5 · Customization Hard Points: 4
  • Weapons: None

Chassis: Action VI Bulk Transport, Edge of the Empire Core Rulebook (adjustments: none). Era notes: The tanks are the newest thing aboard; the keel predates the Withering and the clan bought it as salvage for less than one hold's worth of fuel now sells for. Its real armor is economics — burn a Kajidic barge and your world goes dark next quarter. Using it: The barge is a set, not a combatant: escort jobs, tollgate standoffs, a heist through 10,000 encumbrance of tank maze, or a negotiation where the cargo is the hostage. It cannot fight and barely steers, so every threat to it immediately becomes a social and logistical problem — exactly the kind the Kajidics pay wayfinder crews, no questions attached, to solve. If the clan expects trouble, trouble arrives as a hired escort ship, not a gun bolted to the barge.

docs.title: The Awakening
docs.text:
The Force is coming back. Nobody knows why. Nobody is ready.

For two generations almost no one was born with the gift; for the last twenty years the births have been rising, and no one knows why. The signs are consistent:

  • True dreams.
  • The hearth-sense — reading a room's feeling like weather.
  • Small luck that bends.

There are no schools, no Council, no temple that will take them — at most, rumor of a hidden lineage or two out in the deep systems, not advertising. What there is instead is a galaxy with a generational grudge: households that buried sons over the orders' last war now watch the neighbor's daughter bend luck, and respond with worship, exile, or drowning-fear.

docs.title: What the factions want with the children
docs.text: Faction Wants them as The Provisional Republic A census The Admiralty Assets The Vigil Wards — custody The Inheritors Apprentices The Lamplighters Navigators — quietly. A child who dreams true can feel a dead lane the way old pilots claim to The Kajidics Merchandise The Mandalorian Clans Nothing — they simply adopt them. A foundling who bends luck is just a promising warrior

docs.title: The vacuum the Adjournment left
docs.text: With the Council out of session, no one alive can admit one of them to the Jedi Order — and no one has standing to deny them either. The day one of them stands up and says the word aloud, the only body that could rule on the claim is the one it takes three Masters to reconvene.

docs.title: Immi
docs.text: A Force-sensitive player character is fully supported (see Character Creation). Either way, keep one in the party's orbit: Immi Ozha, twelve, a stowaway who turns up in the crew's hold in session one, dreaming loudly of a canyon full of light she has never seen.

docs.title: The Galaxy at 90 AR
docs.text: What daily life looks like ninety years into the Withering.

docs.title: Travel is the defining fact of life
docs.text:
A handful of major lanes still run intermittently; minor routes have decayed past their nav data, and a rutter — an inherited, annotated route-log — is often worth more than the ship carrying it. Starships are heirlooms maintained by devotion, and the few shipyards that still function are strategic prizes worth wars.

News moves by courier packet and arrives months old, already halfway to myth. The old geography has inverted in places: parts of the Core are hollow grandeur — marble senate halls with the power out — while some Rim worlds, forced into self-sufficiency early, have quietly thrived and see no reason to be "reconnected."

docs.title: The Force, remembered wrong
docs.text:
Most living beings have never seen the Force used, and where it is remembered at all, it is remembered as the thing that burned the old galaxy down. The grudge is generational — a ledger of war dead read out at funerals, with Jedi and Sith entered in the same column. Reactions to the gift run superstitious: awe, terror, and, under both, blame.

(Mechanically, this is the witness rule: in this era the Force is not a skill; it is an event.)

docs.title: The economy of leftovers
docs.text:
The Withering built its own institutions in the corners. Nothing new gets manufactured at scale, so the real economy is salvage: junk barons, chop-yards, and scavenger clans stripping the war's leftovers, with the best finds moving through Kajidic markets.

Droids are heirlooms like everything else, and a pre-war droid with an unwiped memory core is a walking archive — which makes old droids quietly precious and occasionally hunted. Ninety years of isolation has splintered Basic into local creoles, so protocol droids and flesh-and-blood interpreters are load-bearing professions again.

docs.title: The two networks that never stopped running
docs.text:
With the HoloNet dead, news moves through:

  • The cantina — where a good rumor is worth a drink minimum, and ships still change hands over sabacc.
  • The swoop circuit — whose racers carry mail, gossip, and contraband between systems. The season standings are the closest thing the galaxy has to a shared broadcast.

docs.title: Terms of the Era
docs.text:
The appendix glossary — the words everyone at the table should end up using without thinking.

Term Meaning AR After Ruusan, the common calendar the Withering The long decline the Ebb / the Awakening The Force's fall and return wayfinder Scout-envoy-archaeologist; the party rutter An inherited, annotated route-log scrip Sector currency first-lighting Fee and honor for reopening a beacon the Adjournment The High Council's vote to suspend itself sine die, 12 AR — the Order itself was never adjourned the Bastion Worlds The shipyard cluster the Admiralty governs the black lanes The unregistered routes that never went dark a posting A Guild bounty, the one writ that still travels the Quiet Deep-rim slang for dead space

docs.title: The Withering
docs.text:
Ninety years, decade by decade — how the galaxy went out like a lamp: not smashed, just left untended.

The thesis of the era

Nobody broke the galaxy — everyone just stopped holding it up.

docs.title: 0 AR — Ruusan
docs.text: Seven battles end the New Sith Wars. Lord Kaan's thought bomb consumes both armies, and a thousand light and dark spirits are bound together in what becomes the Valley of the Jedi. Most of the Jedi Order dies on that world. Publicly, the Sith are extinct. Secretly, Darth Bane walks away with one apprentice and a Rule: two, no more.

docs.title: 0–12 AR — The Reformation and the Adjournment
docs.text:
The Republic demilitarizes in relief, and grief curdles fast into blame: after a thousand years of Sith wars the graves do not distinguish which order dug them, and in the mouths of the bereaved, Jedi and Sith become one curse. What remains of the Order — the old, the healers, the librarians, those who were not at Ruusan — places itself under Senate oversight and tries to continue, and finds no one willing to fund it, house it, or hand it a child.

In 12 AR, too few and too unwelcome to govern anything, the High Council votes to adjourn — itself, not the Order. No council can adjourn a covenant with the Force, and the Masters knew it; what they suspended was governance: admissions, ranks, rulings, the voice. The motion carries with one amendment, easy to miss in the minutes: any three Masters, met together in a temple, may call the Council back into session.

The Council's last act deeds the sealed temples and relics — property, never the calling — to the custodial order that becomes the Vigil; the archives disperse for a safekeeping that becomes scattering. The survivors go where the anger is thinnest and do the only thing left: one master, one or two pupils, wherever a rare gifted child can be found and a family persuaded.

The Order never ends. It thins to a handful of hidden lineages and loses its voice.

docs.title: 12–35 AR — The Long Exhale
docs.text: The fleets are decommissioned faster than anything replaces them, and sector defense devolves to local squadrons. Around 20 AR, one admiral over the shipyard worlds of the Bastion cluster simply declines the recall order, citing piracy — and is quietly ignored. Her heirs never leave.

docs.title: 35–58 AR — The Quiet Ledger
docs.text: No villain kills the HoloNet; appropriations committees do. Relay maintenance lapses sector by sector. Interstellar credit fractures into sector scrip. Long-haul trade privatizes, then localizes, then stops.

docs.title: 58–75 AR — The Drift and the Ebb
docs.text: Rim delegations stop attending a Senate whose sessions cost more to reach than they are worth, and quorum becomes ceremony. Meanwhile Force-sensitive births thin to almost nothing — the Ebb — and the few children born with the gift are hidden by their own families, because the surest way to lose a child is to let the neighbors hear the word Jedi. The hidden lineages starve for pupils, and most of them snap. It takes a generation for anyone to notice the Ebb at all, because there is no longer an Order counting.

docs.title: 75–90 AR — The Dimming and the Awakening
docs.text:
The war generation begins to die. News travels by courier and arrives as rumor, and on ten thousand worlds the Jedi and Sith pass from testimony into story. Then, in the same years, the Ebb reverses: Force-sensitive children are born in rising numbers, the oldest of them now young adults. The galaxy is forgetting the Force at exactly the moment the Force remembers the galaxy.

In 90 AR, hyperspace beacon Vesta-9, dark for sixty years, relights. Nobody admits to lighting it.

docs.title: Living memory at 90 AR
docs.text:
For humans, Ruusan is now a childhood memory of the very old: the last people who watched the armies pass are in their nineties, and they are dying this decade. For longer-lived species the ledger is different — a Wookiee who fought there is barely middle-aged, a Duros merchant remembers the Republic solvent, a Hutt remembers it whole. Galactic memory is stratified by species, and humans are already mythologizing what a living eyewitness two docks over can flatly contradict.

History here is not yet archaeology. It can still be interviewed — and the interviews disagree.

(At the table, that sentence is a mechanic: see Lore Fragments.)
